entries.source: ISO 24495-1:2023; Plain Writing Act of 2010 (US); Consumer Rights Act 2015 (UK); GDPR Article 12.

entries.title: Front-loaded sentences
entries.numbers: GOV.UK: page titles 65 characters or less, frontloaded. Nielsen Norman Group: the 40 to 60 characters of a page title are the ones that affect search ranking and clicks.
entries.source: GOV.UK content and publishing guidance, A to Z style guide; Loranger and Nielsen, Microcontent, Nielsen Norman Group (2017).

entries.title: Active voice
entries.numbers: Pullum (2009): of the four pairs of examples in the Use the active voice section, three are misidentified as passive.
entries.source: William Strunk Jr and E. B. White, The Elements of Style; Geoffrey K. Pullum, 50 Years of Stupid Grammar Advice, The Chronicle of Higher Education, 17 April 2009.

entries.title: Reading level targeting
entries.numbers: WCAG 2.2 SC 3.1.5 Reading Level is Level AAA and names lower secondary education level, which WCAG defines, following the UNESCO education classification, as the two or three year period beginning after six years of school and ending nine years after the start of primary education. UK Home Office guidance: maximum reading age 9.
entries.source: Flesch (1948); Kincaid et al (1975); Gunning (1952); McLaughlin (1969); W3C WCAG 2.2 SC 3.1.5; UK Home Office User-Centred Design Manual.

entries.title: Scannability
entries.numbers: Morkes and Nielsen (1997): 79 per cent of test users always scanned a new page, 16 per cent read word by word; concise 58 per cent better, scannable 47 per cent, objective 27 per cent, all three combined 124 per cent. Nielsen (2008), on Weinreich et al, ACM Transactions on the Web 2:1: 28 per cent of words read at the maximum, about 20 per cent more realistically.
entries.source: Morkes and Nielsen (1997); Nielsen, How Little Do Users Read? (2008); Pernice, F-Shaped Pattern of Reading on the Web, Nielsen Norman Group (2017).

entries.title: Meaningful headings
entries.numbers: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.6 Headings and Labels, Level AA.
entries.source: W3C, WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.6; Material Design 3 content style guide; Morkes and Nielsen (1997).

entries.title: Link text that works out of context
entries.numbers: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.4 Link Purpose (In Context) is Level A. SC 2.4.9 Link Purpose (Link Only) is the stricter version of the same requirement, at Level AAA.
entries.source: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.2, Success Criterion 2.4.4.

entries.title: Chunking (content)
entries.numbers: Miller (1956), Psychological Review 63, pp. 81-97. Cowan (2001), Behavioral and Brain Sciences 24:1, pp. 87-114, argues for a limit closer to four items.
entries.source: Practice: web content design convention. Justification usually credited to George A. Miller (1956), which the paper itself does not support.

entries.title: Terminology consistency
entries.numbers: WCAG 2.2 SC 3.2.4 Consistent Identification, Level AA. ISO 9241-110:2020 sets seven interaction principles; conformity with user expectations is clause 5.3.
entries.source: Jakob Nielsen, 10 Usability Heuristics (1994); W3C WCAG 2.2 SC 3.2.4; ISO 9241-110:2020, interaction principles.

entries.title: Voice and tone matrix
entries.numbers: voiceandtone.com (2012) covered twenty-five content types, from Freddie's Jokes and Success Message at the green end to Failure Message and Compliance Alert at the red end.
entries.source: Kate Kiefer Lee, MailChimp Voice and Tone, voiceandtone.com (2012); Apple Human Interface Guidelines, Writing.

entries.title: Tone in failure states
entries.numbers: MailChimp's archived failure-message page predicted three user feelings, confusion, stress and anger, and gave four tips: be straightforward, be calm, be serious, and offer a solution or next step if possible.
entries.source: Apple Human Interface Guidelines, Writing; Jakob Nielsen, 10 Usability Heuristics (1994), heuristic 9; Kate Kiefer Lee, MailChimp Voice and Tone, voiceandtone.com (2012).

entries.title: Inclusive language
entries.numbers: Kenny et al (2016), Autism: of 502 autistic adults, around 40 per cent endorsed autistic and around 18 per cent endorsed person with autism. A 2023 Dutch survey (PubMed Central PMC10074744) found the reverse locally, with 68.3 per cent of autistic adults preferring person-first wording.
entries.source: Microsoft Writing Style Guide, Bias-free communication; Apple Human Interface Guidelines, Writing; Kenny, Hattersley, Molins, Buckley, Povey and Pellicano, Autism (2016).

entries.title: Numerals, units and localisation
entries.numbers: SI Brochure, ninth edition, section 5.4.3: a space always separates the numerical value from the unit symbol, with exceptions for degree, minute and second of plane angle. ISO 8601-1:2019 sets the year-month-day date form.
entries.source: BIPM, The International System of Units (SI Brochure), 9th edition, section 5.4.3; ISO 8601-1:2019.

entries.title: Truncation strategy
entries.numbers: CSS text-overflow with the ellipsis keyword renders U+2026 HORIZONTAL ELLIPSIS. MDN notes that text-overflow does not force an overflow, and gives overflow hidden with white-space nowrap as the pairing that makes it take effect.
entries.source: CSS text-overflow, documented on MDN; PatternFly content guidance. No single origin.

entries.title: Message hierarchy
entries.numbers: The sort deals a deck of brand attribute cards into three columns, then cuts to roughly three top attributes with supporting words. Published card counts for the deck disagree, so none is given here.
entries.source: Margot Bloomstein, Content Strategy at Work, Morgan Kaufmann (2012).

entries.title: One primary job per page
entries.numbers: Unbounce's stated target for a dedicated landing page is a one to one attention ratio.
entries.source: Oli Gardner / Unbounce, The 7 Principles of Conversion-Centered Design. The broader one-purpose-per-page idea has no single origin.

entries.title: Readable legal and compliance copy
entries.numbers: GDPR Article 12(1). Consumer Rights Act 2015 (UK), sections 64(3) and 68(2). GameStation, 1 April 2010: 7,500 purchases that day, no opt-out clicks.
entries.source: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR), Article 12; Consumer Rights Act 2015 (UK), sections 64 and 68.

entries.title: Conformance levels A, AA, AAA
entries.numbers: WCAG states it is not recommended that Level AAA conformance be required as a general policy for entire sites, because some content cannot satisfy every AAA criterion.
entries.source: W3C, WCAG 2.2 conformance requirements; GOV.UK accessibility requirements guidance.

entries.title: Text contrast minimums
entries.numbers: 4.5:1 normal text, 3:1 large text (AA). 7:1 and 4.5:1 (AAA). Large text is 18pt, or 14pt bold.
entries.source: W3C, WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.3 and 1.4.6, with the derivation given in Understanding SC 1.4.3.

entries.title: Non-text and UI component contrast
entries.numbers: 3:1 for identifying components and their states, and for the parts of graphics needed to understand them.
entries.source: W3C, WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast (Level AA).

entries.title: Resize text to 200 per cent
entries.numbers: 200 per cent, Level AA.
entries.source: W3C, WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.4 Resize Text (Level AA).

entries.title: Text spacing override
entries.numbers: Line height 1.5x font size, paragraph spacing 2x, letter spacing 0.12x, word spacing 0.16x.
entries.source: W3C, WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.12 Text Spacing (Level AA).

entries.title: Reflow at 320 CSS pixels
entries.numbers: 320 CSS pixels wide (horizontal languages) or 256 CSS pixels tall (vertical languages), equivalent to 400 per cent zoom at 1280 pixels.
entries.source: W3C, WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.10 Reflow (Level AA).

entries.title: No colour-only encoding
entries.numbers: Technique G183: where an inline link is distinguished from static text by colour alone, the contrast ratio between link text and surrounding text must be at least 3:1, measured as a difference in relative luminance. Each colour also still has to pass 4.5:1 against the background.
entries.source: W3C, WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.1 Use of Color (Level A); WCAG 2.2 Technique G183.

entries.title: Visible focus indicator
entries.numbers: AAA appearance test: at least the area of a 2 CSS pixel perimeter, and at least 3:1 between focused and unfocused states.
entries.source: W3C, WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.7 (AA), 2.4.11 (AA, new in 2.2) and 2.4.13 (AAA, new in 2.2).

entries.title: Minimum target size
entries.numbers: WCAG: 24 by 24 CSS pixels (AA), 44 by 44 (AAA). Material Design 3: at least 48 by 48dp for touch, 44 by 44dp for pointer, 8dp between targets. Apple's Human Interface Guidelines list a default control size of 44 by 44pt on iOS and iPadOS with a stated minimum of 28 by 28pt.
entries.source: W3C, WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 and 2.5.5; Material Design 3 accessibility guidance; Apple Human Interface Guidelines.

entries.title: Reduced-motion preference
entries.numbers: MDN records prefers-reduced-motion as available across browsers since January 2020. The settings are macOS Accessibility, Reduce motion; iOS Settings, Accessibility, Motion; Windows 11 Accessibility, Visual effects, Animation effects; Android Remove animations.
entries.source: W3C, CSS Media Queries Level 5 (prefers-reduced-motion); WCAG 2.2 SC 2.3.3 (Level AAA); Apple Human Interface Guidelines.

entries.title: Flash and seizure thresholds
entries.numbers: Three general or three red flashes per second. The standard describes the area limit as 25 per cent of any 10 degree visual field, and exempts fine balanced patterns with squares smaller than 0.1 degree.
entries.source: W3C, WCAG 2.2 SC 2.3.1 (Level A) and 2.3.2 (Level AAA); Apple Human Interface Guidelines.

entries.title: Semantic HTML and landmarks
entries.numbers: Eight landmark roles: banner, navigation, search, main, complementary, contentinfo, region, form.
entries.source: W3C, WCAG 2.2 SC 1.3.1 (Level A); WAI-ARIA landmark roles; Material Design 3 accessibility guidance.

entries.title: Heading outline
entries.numbers: Survey base: 1,539 valid responses, December 2023 to January 2024.
entries.source: W3C, WCAG 2.2 SC 1.3.1 and 2.4.6 (Level AA); WebAIM Screen Reader User Survey #10 (2024); Material Design 3 accessibility guidance.

entries.title: Accessible names and descriptions
entries.numbers: Name precedence: aria-labelledby, aria-label, native host language feature, content, tooltip.
entries.source: W3C, Accessible Name and Description Computation 1.2, Working Draft 5 August 2026; WCAG 2.2 SC 4.1.2 (Level A).

entries.title: Form labels and instructions
entries.numbers: 51 per cent of home pages had missing form input labels (WebAIM Million, February 2026).
entries.source: W3C, WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions (Level A); WebAIM Million (February 2026).

entries.title: Alt text decision tree
entries.numbers: Missing alt text on 53.1 per cent of home pages (WebAIM Million, February 2026).
entries.source: W3C WAI, An alt Decision Tree, updated 13 May 2024; WCAG 2.2 SC 1.1.1 (Level A).

entries.title: Language attributes
entries.numbers: 13.5 per cent of home pages missing a document language (WebAIM Million, February 2026).
entries.source: W3C, WCAG 2.2 SC 3.1.1 (Level A) and 3.1.2 (Level AA); WebAIM Million (February 2026).

entries.title: Timeouts and extensions
entries.numbers: At least 20 seconds of warning, adjustment or extension up to ten times, and an exemption above 20 hours (2.2.1). 2.2.6 uses the same 20 hour figure for preserved data.
entries.source: W3C, WCAG 2.2 SC 2.2.1 (Level A) and 2.2.6 (Level AAA).

entries.title: Cognitive accessibility
entries.numbers: Eight objectives in the 2021 W3C Working Group Note.
entries.source: W3C COGA Task Force, Making Content Usable for People with Cognitive and Learning Disabilities, W3C Working Group Note, 29 April 2021.

entries.title: Situational, temporary and permanent impairment
entries.numbers: Microsoft's own sizing of the touch example: in the United States 26,000 people a year suffer loss of upper extremities, and counting temporary and situational impairments the number is greater than 20 million. Microsoft attributes those to the US Census Bureau, the Limbs for Life Foundation, the Amputee Coalition, the CDC and the Disability Statistics Center at UCSF rather than to one study, so quote them as its estimate.
entries.source: Microsoft Design, Inclusive 101 Guidebook (2016) and the Inclusive Design toolkit (inclusive.microsoft.design).

entries.title: Curb-cut effect
entries.numbers: Nine out of ten unencumbered pedestrians (Sarasota shopping mall). Blackwell's endnote traces the figure to a newspaper report, Frank Greve, Curb ramps liberate Americans with disabilities—and everyone else, McClatchy Newspapers, 31 January 2007, so it is journalism rather than a peer-reviewed study and no sample size is given.
entries.source: Angela Glover Blackwell, The Curb-Cut Effect, Stanford Social Innovation Review, Winter 2017 (Vol. 15, No. 1).

entries.title: Testing with assistive technology
entries.numbers: WebAIM's February 2026 scan of a million home pages detected WCAG 2 failures on 95.9 per cent of them, averaging 56.1 errors per page.
entries.source: WebAIM, Screen Reader User Survey #10 (2024) and The WebAIM Million (February 2026).

entries.title: Follow-through and overlapping action
entries.numbers: Material Design 1 choreography: begin each item's staggered entrance no more than 20ms apart.
entries.source: Frank Thomas and Ollie Johnston, The Illusion of Life: Disney Animation (1981); Material Design 1 choreography guidance (Google)

entries.title: Slow in and slow out
entries.numbers: Material Design 1 curves, read from Google's Duration and easing page: standard cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 0.2, 1); deceleration cubic-bezier(0, 0, 0.2, 1); acceleration cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 1, 1); sharp cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 0.6, 1).
entries.source: Frank Thomas and Ollie Johnston, The Illusion of Life: Disney Animation (1981); Material Design 1 duration and easing guidance (Google)

entries.title: Timing
entries.numbers: Nielsen's response limits: 0.1s, 1s, 10s. Google's RAIL model: complete a transition initiated by user input within 100ms.
entries.source: Frank Thomas and Ollie Johnston, The Illusion of Life: Disney Animation (1981); Jakob Nielsen, Response Times: The 3 Important Limits (1993)

entries.title: Duration guidelines
entries.numbers: Material Design 1: mobile 300ms typical, 375ms large or full-screen, 225ms entering, 195ms leaving, tablet about 30 per cent longer (300ms becomes 390ms), wearable about 30 per cent shorter (300ms becomes 210ms), desktop 150 to 200ms, transitions exceeding 400ms may feel too slow. Material Design 2 component figures: switch 100ms, bottom sheet or chip 250ms expanding and 200ms collapsing, floating action button into a full-screen dialog 300ms expanding and 250ms collapsing. Material Design 3 tokens: short1 50ms, short2 100ms, short3 150ms, short4 200ms, medium1 250ms, medium2 300ms, medium3 350ms, medium4 400ms, long1 450ms, long2 500ms, long3 550ms, long4 600ms, extraLong1 700ms, extraLong2 800ms, extraLong3 900ms, extraLong4 1000ms.
entries.source: Material Design 1 duration and easing guidance (Google); Material Design 2 Speed guidance (Google); Material Design 3 duration tokens as published in the Material Components for Android documentation

entries.title: Easing curves (standard, decelerate, accelerate)
entries.numbers: Material 1: standard cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 0.2, 1), deceleration cubic-bezier(0, 0, 0.2, 1), acceleration cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 1, 1), sharp cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 0.6, 1). Material 3 (Android attributes): standard cubic-bezier(0.2, 0, 0, 1), standard decelerate cubic-bezier(0, 0, 0, 1), standard accelerate cubic-bezier(0.3, 0, 1, 1), emphasized decelerate cubic-bezier(0.05, 0.7, 0.1, 1), emphasized accelerate cubic-bezier(0.3, 0, 0.8, 0.15); linear cubic-bezier(0, 0, 1, 1); emphasized itself is published as the path M 0,0 C 0.05, 0, 0.133333, 0.06, 0.166666, 0.4 C 0.208333, 0.82, 0.25, 1, 1, 1.
entries.source: Material Design 1 duration and easing guidance (Google); Material Design 3 easing tokens as published in the Material Components for Android documentation

entries.title: Spring physics (stiffness, damping, mass)
entries.numbers: Damping ratio = damping / (2 * sqrt(stiffness * mass)), per Apple's UISpringTimingParameters documentation. A ratio of 1 is critical damping.
entries.source: Apple Developer Documentation, UISpringTimingParameters (init with mass, stiffness, damping and initial velocity)

entries.title: Choreography and staggering
entries.numbers: Material Design 1 choreography: staggered entrances no more than 20ms apart.
entries.source: Material Design 1 choreography and meaningful transitions guidance (Google); Issara Willenskomer, Creating Usability with Motion: The UX in Motion Manifesto (31 March 2017)

entries.title: Spatial model and z-depth
entries.numbers: Material Design 2 default elevation values in dp: dialog 24, modal bottom sheet and navigation drawer 16, pressed floating action button 12, standard bottom sheet and menus 8, resting floating action button and snackbar 6, scrolled top app bar 4, contained button 2, card 1.
entries.source: Material Design 2 elevation guidance (Google)

entries.title: Motion as feedback
entries.numbers: Nielsen: 0.1 second is the limit for feeling that the system is reacting instantaneously. RAIL: process input events within 50ms and complete an input-initiated transition within 100ms.
entries.source: Material Design 2 Understanding motion guidance and Material Design 1 choreography guidance (Google); Apple, Human Interface Guidelines: Motion; Jakob Nielsen, Response Times: The 3 Important Limits (1993); Google, RAIL performance model

entries.title: Masking and clipping reveals
entries.numbers: ViewAnimationUtils.createCircularReveal has been available since API level 21 (Android 5.0).
entries.source: Issara Willenskomer, Creating Usability with Motion: The UX in Motion Manifesto (31 March 2017); Android Developers, reveal or hide a view using animation

entries.title: Idle and loop animation
entries.numbers: Nielsen Norman Group: looped animation for waits of roughly 2 to 10 seconds, percent-done for 10 seconds or more. WCAG 2.2 SC 2.2.2: automatic movement lasting more than five seconds alongside other content needs a pause, stop or hide mechanism.
entries.source: Katie Sherwin, Progress Indicators Make a Slow System Less Insufferable, Nielsen Norman Group (26 October 2014); W3C, WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.2.2

entries.title: Pause, stop, hide for automatic motion
entries.numbers: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.2.2, Level A: more than five seconds of automatic movement presented in parallel with other content requires a pause, stop or hide mechanism.
entries.source: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.2, Success Criterion 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide (Level A)

entries.title: Frame budget and 60fps
entries.numbers: RAIL: produce each animation frame in 10ms or less; 1000/60 is approximately 16ms per frame; process input events within 50ms; complete an input-initiated transition within 100ms.
entries.source: Google, RAIL performance model (web.dev); Apple, WWDC 2018 session 803, Designing Fluid Interfaces

entries.title: Vestibular safety
entries.numbers: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.3.1: no more than three flashes in any one-second period, or flashing below the general flash and red flash thresholds. Apple's spatial guidance: avoid sustained oscillation at frequencies around 0.2Hz.
entries.source: Val Head, Designing Safer Web Animation For Motion Sensitivity, A List Apart (8 September 2015); Apple, Human Interface Guidelines: Motion; W3C, WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.3.1

entries.title: Earcons
entries.numbers: Blattner and colleagues proposed no more than four notes per motive. Brewster, Wright and Edwards keep pitch below about 5 kHz and above about 125 to 150 Hz, use register differences of two to three octaves, leave at least 0.1 seconds between compound components, stagger concurrent earcons by at least 300 ms measured onset to onset, and hold a family to about three values for each of the three main attributes. Five to ten minutes of training is usually enough to reach roughly 80 per cent identification.
entries.source: Blattner, Sumikawa and Greenberg, Earcons and Icons: Their Structure and Common Design Principles, Human-Computer Interaction 4(1), 1989; guidelines refined by Brewster, Wright and Edwards.

entries.title: Auditory icons
entries.numbers: No thresholds are published for auditory icons. The design rule is the mapping, not a level; loudness limits come from platform guidance and from #9758.
entries.source: William W. Gaver, Auditory Icons: Using Sound in Computer Interfaces, Human-Computer Interaction 2(2), 167 to 177 (1986); William W. Gaver, The SonicFinder: An Interface That Uses Auditory Icons, Human-Computer Interaction 4(1) (1989)

entries.title: Sound as confirmation
entries.numbers: Twelve participants, within subjects. Average recovery from a slip-off was 2.00 seconds in the auditory condition against 4.21 seconds in the visual one (p = 0.004), and 1.5 mouse clicks against 5.89 (p = 0.0008). Overall preference for the sonic buttons was significant (p = 0.0003); annoyance was not significantly different either way.
entries.source: Brewster, Wright, Dix and Edwards, The Sonic Enhancement of Graphical Buttons, INTERACT '95, with supporting platform guidance from Apple and Android.

entries.title: Perceived urgency mapping
entries.numbers: Two experimental series, then a final set of thirteen warnings whose predicted urgency rank order correlated highly significantly with the order listeners produced. The paper gives no single urgency formula you can apply off the page, so treat it as a set of directions, not a calculator.
entries.source: Edworthy, Loxley and Dennis, Improving Auditory Warning Design: Relationship between Warning Sound Parameters and Perceived Urgency, Human Factors 33(2), 205-231 (1991). Earlier practical guidance: Patterson, Guidelines for Auditory Warning Systems on Civil Aircraft, CAA Paper 82017 (1982).

entries.title: Mute-first restraint
entries.numbers: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.2 (Level A): the threshold is audio playing automatically for more than 3 seconds. Chrome's autoplay policy shipped in Chrome 66, April 2018.
entries.source: W3C, WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.4.2 Audio Control; Google's published Chrome autoplay policy; Apple Human Interface Guidelines, Playing audio. No single named originator.

entries.title: Loudness normalisation
entries.numbers: EBU R 128: programme loudness minus 23 LUFS; tolerance plus or minus 0.5 LU (plus or minus 1 LU for live); maximum true peak minus 1 dBTP; measured to ITU-R BS.1770. First published August 2010; version 5.0 November 2023.
entries.source: EBU Recommendation R 128, Loudness normalisation and permitted maximum level of audio signals (EBU, 2010; version 5.0, 2023), with supplement R 128 s1 for short-form content; ITU-R BS.1770 for the measurement

entries.title: Haptic vocabulary
entries.numbers: Android says a good keyclick haptic should last 10 to 20 milliseconds, and warns that the actuator may keep ringing for another 20 to 50 milliseconds after a 20 millisecond input.
entries.source: Apple Human Interface Guidelines, Playing haptics; Android developers, Haptics design principles.

entries.title: Tactons (structured tactile messages)
entries.numbers: Brewster and Brown list seven parameters: frequency, amplitude, waveform, duration, rhythm, body location and spatiotemporal pattern. No recognition thresholds are given here; the 2004 paper is a design proposal and the later studies vary by device.
entries.source: Stephen Brewster and Lorna M. Brown, Tactons: Structured Tactile Messages for Non-Visual Information Display, Proceedings of the Fifth Australasian User Interface Conference (AUIC 2004), Dunedin; Lorna M. Brown, Stephen Brewster and Helen Purchase, Multidimensional Tactons for Non-Visual Information Presentation in Mobile Devices, MobileHCI 2006

entries.title: Haptic intensity mapping
entries.numbers: Core Haptics HapticIntensity and HapticSharpness both run 0 to 1, as do attack, decay and release. Android's createOneShot takes an amplitude of 1 to 255, waveform amplitudes run 0 to 255 with 0 meaning the motor is off, and the predefined ladder is EFFECT_TICK, then EFFECT_CLICK, then EFFECT_HEAVY_CLICK.
entries.source: Android developers, Haptics design principles; Apple, Core Haptics and the AHAP file parameter reference.

entries.title: Standard beep patterns for products
entries.numbers: ISO 24500:2010 specifies patterns, not levels. Sound pressure levels for the same signals are in ISO 24501:2010. Alarm and danger signals are excluded and belong to ISO 7731, ISO 8201 and ISO 11429.
entries.source: ISO 24500:2010, Ergonomics, Accessible design, Auditory signals for consumer products (International Organization for Standardization, 2010); ISO 24501:2010 for sound pressure levels

entries.title: Design tokens (global, alias, component)
entries.numbers: The Design Tokens Format Module draft defines the types color, dimension, fontFamily, fontWeight, duration, cubicBezier and number, plus strokeStyle and the composites border, transition, shadow, gradient and typography. A token value can reference another using the syntax {group.token}.
entries.source: Jina Anne, Salesforce Lightning Design System (2014); Nathan Curtis, Tokens in Design Systems, EightShapes (2016); Design Tokens Community Group, Design Tokens Format Module (draft)

entries.title: Theming and modes
entries.numbers: prefers-color-scheme takes the values light and dark, and MDN records it as available across browsers since January 2020. Material 3 defines 26 colour roles, and states that its medium contrast setting provides a minimum contrast ratio of 3:1 and its high contrast setting 7:1.
entries.source: CSS Media Queries Level 5 (prefers-color-scheme); Material Design 3 colour system, Google

entries.title: Colour ramp construction
entries.numbers: Material 3 tonal palettes run 0 to 100 in increments of 10, plus 95, 98 and 99, and Material notes some palettes carry extra values. Material states that tones 50 and 98 give an accessible 3:1 contrast and tones 30 and 98 reach 7:1. Radix guarantees Lc 60 for step 11 and Lc 90 for step 12 against step 2. WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.3 requires 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text at AA.
entries.source: Material Design 3 colour system (HCT and tonal palettes), Google; Radix Colors documentation, Understanding the Scale; WCAG 2.2, W3C (2023, updated 2024)

entries.title: Spacing scale
entries.numbers: Material 3 spacing tokens, read from the tokens page: space0 0dp, space25 2dp, space50 4dp, space75 6dp, space100 8dp, space125 10dp, space150 12dp, space175 14dp, space200 16dp, space250 20dp, space300 24dp, space400 32dp, space450 36dp, space500 40dp, space600 48dp, space700 56dp, space800 64dp, space900 72dp.
entries.source: Material Design 3 spacing guidance, Google; Jina Anne on the Salesforce four-based metric system

entries.title: Type scale (as tokens)
entries.numbers: The golden ratio used in Brown's worked example is 1:1.618.
entries.source: Tim Brown, More Meaningful Typography, A List Apart (3 May 2011), quoting Robert Bringhurst, The Elements of Typographic Style

entries.title: Radius scale
entries.numbers: Material 3's corner radius scale publishes nine named corner values, from no rounding to extra extra large, plus a fully rounded step. Its own guidance is that shape can direct attention, communicate state and express brand.
entries.source: Material Design 3 shape guidance, Google

entries.title: Elevation and shadow scale
entries.numbers: Material 3 defines six elevation levels, numbered 0 to 5.
entries.source: Material Design 3 elevation guidance, Google

entries.title: Motion tokens
entries.numbers: Material 3 durations: short1 50ms, short2 100ms, short3 150ms, short4 200ms, medium1 250ms through medium4 400ms, long1 450ms through long4 600ms, extra-long1 700ms through extra-long4 1000ms. Easing: standard cubic-bezier(0.2, 0, 0, 1), emphasized decelerate cubic-bezier(0.05, 0.7, 0.1, 1), legacy cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 0.2, 1).
entries.source: Material Design 3 motion tokens, Google (material-web token source); Design Tokens Format Module, Design Tokens Community Group

entries.title: Breakpoint tokens
entries.numbers: Bootstrap 5.3 grid breakpoints: xs 0, sm 576px, md 768px, lg 992px, xl 1200px, xxl 1400px.
entries.source: Bootstrap 5.3 documentation, Layout: Breakpoints

entries.title: Atoms, molecules, organisms, templates, pages
entries.numbers: Five stages: atoms, molecules, organisms, templates, pages.
entries.source: Brad Frost, Atomic Design, blog post (10 June 2013) and Atomic Design, book (2016)

entries.title: Documentation as product
entries.numbers: Diataxis defines four documentation types: tutorials, how-to guides, reference and explanation.
entries.source: Daniele Procida, Diataxis; Storybook documentation. The phrase documentation as product is of unclear origin

entries.title: Contribution model
entries.numbers: Four contribution sizes (fixes, small enhancements, large enhancements, new features) and five steps (propose, design, code, document, release).
entries.source: Nathan Curtis, Defining Design System Contributions, EightShapes (14 January 2020)

entries.title: Governance
entries.numbers: Three team models: solitary, centralised, federated.
entries.source: Nathan Curtis, Team Models for Scaling a Design System, EightShapes (17 September 2015)

entries.title: Versioning and deprecation
entries.numbers: Semantic versioning: MAJOR for incompatible API changes, MINOR for backward compatible additions, PATCH for backward compatible fixes.
entries.source: Tom Preston-Werner, Semantic Versioning (semver.org); Design Tokens Format Module, Design Tokens Community Group

entries.title: Adoption measurement
entries.numbers: In Curtis's example objectives, adoption age targets are dependencies no older than six months for flagship products and twelve months for secondary products. These are his illustrative targets, not an industry standard.
entries.source: Nathan Curtis, Measuring Design System Success (9 June 2017) and Adopting Design Systems (28 June 2017), EightShapes

entries.title: Accessibility baked into components
entries.numbers: WCAG 2.2 became a W3C Recommendation on 5 October 2023, with an updated version published on 12 December 2024. SC 1.4.3 requires 4.5:1 contrast for normal text and 3:1 for large text at AA. SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) requires pointer targets of at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels at AA, with five exceptions: spacing, equivalent, inline, user agent control and essential.
entries.source: W3C, WCAG 2.2 (Recommendation 5 October 2023, updated 12 December 2024); W3C Web Accessibility Initiative, ARIA Authoring Practices Guide

entries.title: Consistency versus local optimisation
entries.numbers: Jonathan Grudin, Communications of the ACM, volume 32, issue 10, pages 1164-1173, October 1989.
entries.source: Jonathan Grudin, The Case Against User Interface Consistency, Communications of the ACM 32(10), 1164-1173 (1989)

entries.title: Design linting
entries.numbers: Stylelint states it has over 100 built-in rules for modern CSS syntax and features, and supports plugins for custom ones.
entries.source: Stylelint documentation; equivalent lint plugins in design tools

entries.title: Visual regression testing
entries.numbers: BackstopJS defaults: misMatchThreshold 0.1 per cent of pixels before a test fails, and requireSameDimensions true, so a screenshot of different dimensions fails regardless of pixel difference.
entries.source: BackstopJS (garris/BackstopJS) documentation; the practice is standard across tools such as this one

entries.title: Performance as a design constraint
entries.numbers: RAIL: respond to input within 100 ms; produce each animation frame in 10 ms or less against a 16 ms hardware frame; do deferred work in 50 ms chunks; load and be interactive in 5 seconds or less on mid-range mobile over slow 3G. web.dev's worked example budget: under 170 KB of compressed critical-path resources. Nielsen's limits: 0.1 s feels instant, 1 s keeps thought unbroken, 10 s is the limit of attention.
entries.source: Tim Kadlec, Setting a performance budget (27 January 2013); Google's RAIL model on web.dev; Jakob Nielsen, Response Times: The 3 Important Limits, after Miller (1968) and Card, Robertson and Mackinlay (1991).

entries.title: Largest Contentful Paint
entries.numbers: Good: 2.5 seconds or less. Needs improvement: between 2.5 and 4.0 seconds. Poor: greater than 4.0 seconds. Assessed at the 75th percentile of page loads, segmented into mobile and desktop.
entries.source: Google Chrome team, Largest Contentful Paint documentation on web.dev; part of Core Web Vitals.

entries.title: Interaction to Next Paint
entries.numbers: Good: 200 milliseconds or less. Needs improvement: between 200 and 500 milliseconds. Poor: above 500 milliseconds. Assessed at the 75th percentile. INP replaced First Input Delay as a Core Web Vital on 12 March 2024.
entries.source: Google Chrome team, Interaction to Next Paint documentation on web.dev.

entries.title: Cumulative Layout Shift
entries.numbers: Good: 0.1 or less. Needs improvement: greater than 0.1 up to 0.25. Poor: greater than 0.25. Assessed at the 75th percentile. Session window: shifts less than 1 second apart, maximum window 5 seconds.
entries.source: Google Chrome team, Cumulative Layout Shift documentation on web.dev.

entries.title: Above-the-fold weight budget
entries.numbers: RFC 6928 initial window: min(10 x MSS, max(2 x MSS, 14600 bytes)). web.dev example critical-path budget: under 170 KB of critical-path resources, compressed and minified, on a 3G assumption.
entries.source: IETF RFC 6928, Increasing TCP's Initial Window (2013); Google, Performance budgets 101, web.dev. There is no published standard using the phrase 'above-the-fold weight budget'.

entries.title: Font loading strategy and subsetting
entries.numbers: MDN states the block and swap durations are user-agent defined, described only as 'short' and 'extremely small'. Firefox exposes them as the preferences gfx.downloadable_fonts.fallback_delay and fallback_delay_short.
entries.source: W3C CSS Fonts Module Level 4, font-display descriptor.

entries.title: Layout-shift prevention
entries.numbers: See entry 800 for the CLS thresholds this prevents breaching: good is 0.1 or less.
entries.source: Google Chrome team, Optimize CLS guidance on web.dev.

entries.title: Skeletons versus spinners
entries.numbers: Viget (2017, n=136, split 39 skeleton, 39 spinner, 58 blank): agreed loading was quick, 59 per cent skeleton, 66 per cent blank, 74 per cent spinner; perceived wait 2.82 s, 2.29 s and 2.41 s in the same order. Chung (2018, n=80) reports the skeleton best on perceived duration on mobile and the blank control worst.
entries.source: Luke Wroblewski, Mobile Design Details: Avoid The Spinner, 17 September 2013; Kathryn Faulkner and Katherine Olvera, A Bone to Pick with Skeleton Screens, Viget, 19 October 2017; Bill Chung, Everything you need to know about skeleton screens, UX Collective, 2018; Tim Kadlec, Effective Skeleton Screens, 2 November 2020.

entries.title: Pointer versus touch input
entries.numbers: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), level AA: targets for pointer inputs are at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, with limited exceptions. SC 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced), level AAA: at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels.
entries.source: W3C Media Queries Level 4 (pointer, hover, any-pointer, any-hover); W3C WCAG 2.2 for the target size figures.

entries.title: Hover, focus, active and visited states
entries.numbers: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.13 Focus Appearance, level AAA: the indicator is at least as large as a 2 CSS pixel thick perimeter of the component and has a contrast ratio of at least 3:1. SC 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), level AA: a focused component must not be entirely hidden by author content.
entries.source: CSS link pseudo-classes, documented on MDN; W3C WCAG 2.2 for the focus criteria.

entries.title: Scroll performance
entries.numbers: RAIL sets 10 ms of work per animation frame against a 16 ms budget on a 60 Hz display, leaving the browser the rest.
entries.source: MDN, addEventListener passive option; Google, RAIL model on web.dev.

entries.title: Dark mode implementation
entries.numbers: Material Design 2: dark surface #121212; at least 15.8:1 contrast between white body text and the surface, which keeps body text above WCAG AA's 4.5:1 even on the lightest 24dp surface; elevation overlay from 0 per cent at 0dp to 16 per cent at 24dp; text opacity 87 / 60 / 38 per cent.
entries.source: Material Design 2, Dark theme guidance (m2.material.io). Material 2 is no longer maintained; the numbers remain the clearest published set.

entries.title: Share and Open Graph image design
entries.numbers: Meta recommends at least 1200 by 630 pixels, a minimum of 600 by 315 for the larger card treatment, an absolute minimum of 200 by 200, and an aspect ratio close to 1.91:1. The Open Graph protocol itself specifies no size.
entries.source: The Open Graph protocol, ogp.me, created at Facebook; Meta for Developers, sharing best practices for images.

entries.title: Favicon and app icon set
entries.numbers: Original favicon: 16 by 16 pixels, favicon.ico, in the site root. The apple-touch-icon sizes in common use are 152, 167 and 180 pixels square, and Android manifest icons are usually supplied in multiples of 48 pixels with 192 as the practical minimum. Those two sets are conventions rather than current published requirements.
entries.source: Microsoft, Internet Explorer 5 (March 1999) for the original; the touch and manifest icon sizes are long-standing platform conventions rather than figures in Apple's current guidelines.

entries.title: 404, error and offline pages
entries.numbers: HTTP 404 Not Found and 410 Gone, as defined in RFC 9110 sections 15.5.5 and 15.5.11.
entries.source: IETF RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics (2022), sections 15.5.5 and 15.5.11.

entries.title: Viewport meta tag and user zoom
entries.numbers: MDN's illustration of the virtual viewport: a 640 pixel screen rendering pages at 980 pixels. WCAG requires a minimum of 2x scaling, per MDN's warning, which cites Success Criterion 1.4.4 Resize Text; MDN calls 5x the better target.
entries.source: MDN Web Docs, meta name=viewport, which cites CSS Viewport Module Level 1; W3C WCAG Success Criterion 1.4.4 Resize Text for the zoom requirement.

entries.title: Image format and compression choice
entries.numbers: MDN reports lossy WebP as on average 25 to 35 per cent smaller than JPEG at similar quality, lossless WebP as typically 26 per cent smaller than PNG, and AVIF as reaching a median 50 per cent reduction on a JPEG set where WebP reached 30 per cent.
entries.source: MDN Web Docs, Image file type and format guide.

entries.title: Brand attributes
entries.numbers: Aaker (1997) reports five dimensions: sincerity, excitement, competence, sophistication, ruggedness.
entries.source: Jennifer L. Aaker, Dimensions of Brand Personality, Journal of Marketing Research 34:3 (1997)

entries.title: Naming
entries.numbers: Abercrombie sets four classes in ascending order of protection: generic, descriptive, suggestive, arbitrary or fanciful.
entries.source: Abercrombie & Fitch Co. v. Hunting World, Inc., 537 F.2d 4 (2d Cir. 1976)

entries.title: Lettermark
entries.numbers: IBM eight-bar logotype introduced 1972, sometimes rendered in thirteen bars; IBM Blue given as Pantone 2718C.
entries.source: IBM corporate history, The IBM logo; Paul Rand (1956, 1972)

entries.title: Abstract mark
entries.numbers: Davidson's final invoice for the swoosh was 35 US dollars (1971).
entries.source: Paul Rand, Logos, Flags, and Escutcheons (1991); Nike swoosh commission, 1971

entries.title: Combination mark
entries.numbers: NASA left-aligned configuration: 1.5 N clear space between the vertical divider rule and the insignia; 2 N minimum clear space on the exterior borders of all configurations.
entries.source: NASA Brand Guidelines, Identifier Configurations

entries.title: Dynamic identity
entries.numbers: MIT Media Lab 2011 system: over 40,000 permutations.
entries.source: MIT Media Lab identity, Richard The, E Roon Kang and Willy Sengewald (2011); replaced by Pentagram (2014)

entries.title: Memorability
entries.numbers: Blake, Nazarian and Castel (2015): 1 of 85 participants drew the Apple logo correctly; fewer than half identified the correct logo among alternatives.
entries.source: Paul Rand (1991); A. B. Blake, M. Nazarian and A. D. Castel, The Apple of the mind's eye, Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology (2015)

entries.title: Scalability
entries.numbers: Android adaptive icons: layers 108 x 108 dp, masked to a maximum of 72 x 72 dp, with a 66 x 66 dp safe zone never clipped by an OEM mask. Material system icons are displayed at 24 x 24 dp.
entries.source: Android Developers, adaptive icon specification; Google, Material Design system icon guidance

entries.title: Small-size test
entries.numbers: Material system icons: 24 x 24 dp grid, 20 x 20 dp live area, 2 dp padding. Android adaptive icon safe zone: 66 x 66 dp within a 108 x 108 dp layer.
entries.source: Paul Rand (1991); Google, Material Design system icon guidance

entries.title: Clear space and minimum size
entries.numbers: NASA insignia protected space: minimum 1 N from the edge of the sphere. Identifier configurations: 2 N minimum on exterior borders. Left-aligned configuration: 1.5 N between vertical divider and insignia.
entries.source: NASA Brand Guidelines, Protected space and minimum size

entries.title: Brand architecture (branded house, endorsed, house of brands)
entries.numbers: Olins (1989) sets three structures: monolithic, endorsed, branded.
entries.source: Wally Olins, Corporate Identity (1989); David A. Aaker and Erich Joachimsthaler, Brand Leadership (2000)

entries.title: Colour ownership
entries.numbers: Qualitex Co. v. Jacobson Products Co., 514 U.S. 159, decided 28 March 1995. Cadbury's mark specified Pantone 2685C; refused on the predominant colour wording, [2013] EWCA Civ 1174. Louboutin: Pantone 18-1663TP, CJEU Case C-163/16 (2018).
entries.source: Qualitex Co. v. Jacobson Products Co., 514 U.S. 159 (1995); Nestle v Cadbury [2013] EWCA Civ 1174; Louboutin v Van Haren, CJEU C-163/16 (2018)

entries.title: Typographic voice
entries.numbers: New Transport was released with six new weights (GDS blog, 5 July 2012).
entries.source: Government Digital Service, A few notes on typography, 5 July 2012; NASA Brand Guidelines typography section

entries.title: Iconography system
entries.numbers: Material system icons: 24 x 24 dp grid, 20 x 20 dp live area, 2 dp padding per side; keylines square 18 x 18 dp, circle 20 dp diameter, vertical rectangle 16 dp wide by 20 dp high, horizontal rectangle 20 dp wide by 16 dp high.
entries.source: Google, Material Design system icon guidance (Material Design 2 and 3)

entries.title: Sonic identity
entries.numbers: NBC chimes: registered 4 April 1950, registration no. 523,616, notes G, E, C. THX Deep Note: created late 1982, US sound trade mark registered 1992, 30 voices over seven measures, initial range 200 to 400 Hz spreading over three octaves.
entries.source: NBC chimes US service mark registration (1950); James A. Moorer, THX Deep Note (1982), US sound trade mark (1992)

entries.title: Tone of voice
entries.numbers: NN/g tone-of-voice study: 50 respondents, five-point Likert scales, differences of about 0.5 to 1 point, significant at p < 0.05.
entries.source: Kate Moran, The Four Dimensions of Tone of Voice, Nielsen Norman Group, 17 July 2016

entries.title: Evolution versus revolution in rebrands
entries.numbers: Gap: new logo on the website in early October 2010, reversal announced 11 October 2010. Tropicana: new pack 8 January 2009, sales reported down about 20 per cent by late February 2009, reversal announced 23 February 2009. Consignia: about £2 million spent on becoming Consignia, of which £500,000 was the name itself; reverting reported as likely to top £1 million (UK press, June 2002).
entries.source: Paul Rand (1991); Gap logo withdrawal (2010); Tropicana packaging reversal (2009); UK press coverage of Consignia (June 2002)

entries.title: Trademark and cultural checks
entries.numbers: Nice Classification: 45 classes, 1 to 34 goods, 35 to 45 services; Nice Agreement concluded 15 June 1957.
entries.source: WIPO, Nice Classification (Nice Agreement, 15 June 1957); Snopes fact-check on the Chevrolet Nova

entries.title: The book as an object
entries.numbers: Van de Graaf canon: margins of one-ninth and two-ninths of the page. At a 2:3 page proportion the margins fall in the ratio 2:3:4:6 (inner:top:outer:bottom), and the height of the type area equals the width of the page.
entries.source: Jan Tschichold, The Form of the Book (English edition 1991), building on J. A. van de Graaf and Raul Rosarivo

entries.title: Front matter, body, back matter
entries.numbers: Chicago 1.7 and 1.8: roman numerals for front matter, arabic numerals for text and back matter.
entries.source: The Chicago Manual of Style, 18th edition, chapter 1 (sections 1.3 to 1.77)

entries.title: Paper choice, weight and opacity
entries.numbers: ISO 536 gives grammage in g/m2. ISO 534 gives thickness in microns. ISO 2471 gives opacity as a percentage.
entries.source: ISO 536, ISO 534 and ISO 2471 (paper test methods)

entries.title: Imposition
entries.numbers: Folding gives pages in multiples of four. Common offset sections are 8, 16 and 32 pages.
entries.source: Standard print production practice; no single originator

entries.title: Trim, bleed and safety margin
entries.numbers: UK and European printers commonly ask for 3 mm bleed. Mixam's UK guidance asks for 3 mm bleed on every product except hardcover covers, which need 20 mm, and a quiet area of at least 5 mm inside the trim edge.
entries.source: Printer specification convention; no single standard body

entries.title: Total ink limit
entries.numbers: The limit belongs to the profile, not to the press in general. ECI publishes two profiles for the same European coated condition, FOGRA39L: ISO Coated v2 (ECI), and ISO Coated v2 300% (ECI), the second built to a lower 300 per cent ceiling for web offset. Printing United Alliance quotes 320 per cent for sheetfed coated (GRACoL), 300 to 320 per cent for heatset web and 300 per cent for SWOP, and calls those industry averages.
entries.source: ISO 12647-2 printing conditions and their characterisation data; ECI offset profile documentation; Printing United Alliance guidance on ink limits

entries.title: Spot colours and specials
entries.numbers: The most-quoted published figure is that about 30 per cent of the system's 1,114 spot colours, counted as of the year 2000, cannot be simulated in CMYK. It is tied to that year and that library size, and the library has grown a great deal since, so treat it as an order of magnitude rather than a current statistic.
entries.source: Lawrence Herbert, Pantone Matching System, launched 1963

entries.title: Screen ruling and halftones
entries.numbers: Trade figures commonly quoted: newsprint around 60 to 85 lpi, uncoated offset around 85 to 133 lpi, coated stock 120 to 150 lpi and above, with high-quality colour work running 150 to 300 lpi.
entries.source: Standard offset practice; halftone screening dates to the nineteenth century, exact originator contested

entries.title: Moire
entries.numbers: In conventional CMYK screening the strong inks are separated by 30 degrees, with yellow offset by about 15 degrees from its neighbours. Specific angle assignments vary by supplier and RIP.
entries.source: Optical interference; standard prepress practice for screen angles

entries.title: DPI versus PPI
entries.numbers: Quality factor of 1.5 to 2 times the screen ruling. At 150 lpi that gives 225 to 300 ppi at final printed size.
entries.source: Standard prepress practice (the quality factor rule); no single originator

entries.title: Prepress checklist
entries.numbers: PDF/X is standardised as ISO 15930. PDF/X-1a requires CMYK or spot colour with flattened transparency; PDF/X-4 permits live transparency and ICC-based colour.
entries.source: ISO 15930 (PDF/X); standard prepress practice

entries.title: Cost consequences of design choices
entries.numbers: Folded sheets give pages in multiples of four; offset work is usually planned in 8, 16 or 32 page sections.
entries.source: Standard print production economics; no single originator

entries.title: Dot gain (tone value increase)
entries.numbers: Gain is largest around the middle of the tonal range and depends heavily on stock. ISO 12647-2:2004 names a set of aim curves, A to F, usually quoted as the gain measured at a 40 per cent patch. ECI's offset documentation gives curve A as 13 per cent, curve B as 16, curve C as 19 and curve D as 22. Coated paper types 1 and 2 run to curve A for cyan, magenta and yellow and curve B for black; wood-free uncoated white runs to curve C and curve D. The standard is paywalled, so get the curve for your job from the printer.
entries.source: ISO 12647-2 (tone value increase for offset processes), as reported in ECI offset profile documentation; dot gain is the older trade term

entries.title: Identification signage
entries.numbers: ADA 2010, 703.2.5: raised characters 5/8 in (16 mm) minimum to 2 in (51 mm) maximum, measured on the uppercase I. ADA 407.2.3.1: lift floor designations 2 in (51 mm) minimum.
entries.source: David Gibson, The Wayfinding Handbook (Princeton Architectural Press, 2009); 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design, 216.2 and 703.

entries.title: Viewing distance to letter-height ratio
entries.numbers: USSC Foundation: legibility index 30 ft per inch of cap height, multiplied by 0.83 in moderate visual complexity and 0.67 in high complexity. CIDEA, University at Buffalo (2010): 35 ft per inch. Bertucci and Crawford (2015): all-caps text needs about 15 per cent more height than mixed case. ADA 2010 Table 703.5.5, for characters mounted 40 in to 70 in above the floor: 5/8 in (16 mm) minimum up to a viewing distance of 72 in, then 5/8 in plus 1/8 in (3.2 mm) per foot of viewing distance beyond 72 in.
entries.source: Andrew Bertucci, Sign Legibility: Rules of Thumb (United States Sign Council Foundation, 2006); Bertucci and Crawford, Best Practice Standards for On-Premise Signs (2015); 2010 ADA Standards, Table 703.5.5.

entries.title: Illumination and contrast in situ
entries.numbers: Approved Document M Volume 2 (2015 edition incorporating 2020 and 2024 amendments), clause 0.26: LRV difference greater than 30 points; minimum 20 points where illuminance on surfaces is greater than 200 lux; 15 points where door opening furniture projects beyond the face of the door and creates its own shade. ADA 2010, 703.5.1: non-glare finish, light on dark or dark on light. Kuhn, Garvey and Pietrucha (1997) report that an on-premise sign reads best when the luminance ratio between the sign and its characters is about 12 to 1.
entries.source: Approved Document M, Volume 2 (2015 with 2024 amendments), clause 0.26; 2010 ADA Standards, 703.5.1; John Bullough, Factors Affecting Sign Visibility, Conspicuity and Legibility, Interdisciplinary Journal of Signage and Wayfinding, volume 1 issue 2.

entries.title: Material durability and weathering
entries.numbers: ASTM G154 defines UVA-340 and UVB-313 fluorescent lamps used across eight numbered exposure cycles: UVA-340 is specified in cycles 1, 4, 6 and 7, UVB-313 in cycles 2, 3, 5 and 8. Q-Lab describes UVA-340 as the closest match to the shortwave ultraviolet in noon summer sunlight, and UVB-313 as carrying more high-energy UVB than anything reaching the earth's surface.
entries.source: ASTM G154, ASTM G155 and the ISO 4892 series. No authority publishes a lifespan for signs in service.

entries.title: Mounting height and sightlines
entries.numbers: ADA 2010: tactile characters 48 in (1220 mm) minimum to 60 in (1525 mm) maximum above finished floor, measured to character baselines (703.4.1); visual characters at least 40 in (1015 mm) above the floor (703.5.6); objects with leading edges between 27 in (685 mm) and 80 in (2030 mm) may protrude 4 in (100 mm) maximum into a circulation path (307.2); vertical clearance 80 in (2030 mm) minimum (307.4).
entries.source: 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design, sections 307.2, 307.4, 703.4.1 and 703.5.6.

entries.title: Universal symbols
entries.numbers: ADA 2010, 703.6.1: pictogram field height 6 in (150 mm) minimum, with no characters or braille inside the field. AIGA/DOT: 34 symbols in 1974, 50 after the 1979 additions.
entries.source: AIGA and the US Department of Transportation, Symbol Signs (1974, extended 1979); ISO 7001 (first published October 1980, current edition 2023); ISO 22727:2007; ISO 9186-1; 2010 ADA Standards, 703.6.

entries.title: Multilingual signage
entries.numbers: Jamson, Tate and Jamson (2005): one-line and two-line monolingual signs and two-line bilingual signs read with no measurable disruption to driving; four-line signs, monolingual or bilingual, produced a significant speed reduction and increased headway.
entries.source: S. L. Jamson, F. N. Tate and A. H. Jamson, Evaluating the effects of bilingual traffic signs on driver performance and safety, Ergonomics 48(15), 2005, pages 1734 to 1748.

entries.title: Evacuation and safety signage
entries.numbers: ISO 7010 first published October 2003, current edition 2019. ISO 3864 colour meanings: red for prohibition and fire equipment, blue for mandatory action, yellow for warning, green for safe condition.
entries.source: ISO 3864-1 and ISO 7010; Health and Safety (Safety Signs and Signals) Regulations 1996, with HSE guidance L64, third edition (2015).

entries.title: Exhibition sequencing and dwell time
entries.numbers: Serrell (1998, 110 exhibitions): average visit about 20 minutes. Later sample of 50 exhibitions: average sweep rate index 300 sq ft per minute, average diligent visitors 26 per cent. Exceptionally thoroughly used means a sweep rate below 300 and more than 51 per cent diligent visitors, a benchmark derived from the 1991 Darkened Waters study at the Pratt Museum. Seven of the 50 met it.
entries.source: Beverly Serrell, Paying Attention: Visitors and Museum Exhibitions (American Association of Museums, 1998), and her follow-up Paying More Attention to Paying Attention (informalscience.org, March 2010).

entries.title: Tactile and braille signage
entries.numbers: ADA 2010: raised characters 5/8 in (16 mm) to 2 in (51 mm), based on the uppercase I (703.2.5); stroke thickness 15 per cent of character height maximum (703.2.6); braille contracted Grade 2, dot base diameter 0.059 to 0.063 in (1.5 to 1.6 mm) (703.3.1); tactile characters mounted 48 in (1220 mm) to 60 in (1525 mm) above the floor, measured to character baselines (703.4.1).
entries.source: 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design, sections 703.1, 703.2, 703.3, 703.4 and 407.2.3.1.

entries.title: Anthropometrics
entries.numbers: ISO 7250 defines basic human body measurements for technological design. ISO 15535 sets general requirements for anthropometric databases.
entries.source: Henry Dreyfuss, Designing for People (1955) and The Measure of Man (1960); ISO 7250; Gilbert S. Daniels, WADC Technical Note 53-7 (1952)

entries.title: Ergonomics
entries.numbers: ISO 6385 sets out ergonomics principles in the design of work systems. The IEA's three domains are physical, cognitive and organisational.
entries.source: International Ergonomics Association definition; ISO 6385

entries.title: Reach envelopes
entries.numbers: SAE J287 gives hand reach envelopes for three-finger, extended-finger and full-hand grasp, referenced to a vehicle seating configuration. Issued July 1976; current revision November 2022.
entries.source: Ralph M. Barnes, Motion and Time Study (normal and maximum working areas); SAE J287, Driver Hand Control Reach

entries.title: Grip and control design
entries.numbers: Kong and Lowe (2005) found 30, 35 and 40 mm cylindrical handles rated significantly more comfortable than smaller or larger ones, with the comfort-maximising diameter calculated at 19.7 per cent of hand length. CCOHS guidance gives 30 to 50 mm for a power grip, with 40 mm as a general figure.
entries.source: John Napier, The prehensile movements of the human hand, Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery 38-B(4), 902-913 (1956); Yong-Ku Kong and Brian D. Lowe, Optimal cylindrical handle diameter for grip force tasks, International Journal of Industrial Ergonomics 35(6), 495-507 (2005)

entries.title: Tolerances and fit
entries.numbers: ISO 2768-1 tolerance classes f, m, c and v. For the medium class, permissible deviation is plus or minus 0.1 mm over 3 to 6 mm nominal length and plus or minus 0.2 mm over 6 to 30 mm.
entries.source: ISO 286 (geometrical product specifications: limits and fits); ISO 2768-1 (general tolerances for linear and angular dimensions)

entries.title: Repairability
entries.numbers: French repairability index: score from 0 to 10, five criteria, in force from 1 January 2021, initially covering five product categories. iFixit repairability scores also run 0 to 10, zero meaning unrepairable and ten easiest to repair.
entries.source: French repairability index (in force 1 January 2021); Regulation (EU) 2024/1781 (Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation); iFixit repairability scoring

entries.title: Weight and balance
entries.numbers: For manual lifting, the revised NIOSH lifting equation uses a load constant of 23 kg, described by NIOSH as safe under ideal conditions for 75 per cent of women and 90 per cent of men before any of the six task multipliers are applied.
entries.source: Mechanics of moment and centre of gravity (standard engineering); NIOSH revised lifting equation for the load constant

entries.title: Factor of safety
entries.numbers: I have not stated typical values here. Wikipedia lists figures such as 2.0 for building structural members and 1.25 for landing gear, but attributes them to general engineering practice without naming a code, so they are not safe to quote as standards.
entries.source: Standard engineering practice; specific design factors are mandated by application-specific codes rather than by one general standard

entries.title: Control-display compatibility
entries.numbers: Chapanis and Lindenbaum (1959): 15 subjects, four wooden stove models, 80 consecutive trials. The abstract reports significant improvement across the 80 trials but none in the second half, and the ranking of arrangements was analysed on trials 41 to 80. It also reports that a second arrangement was significantly worse than the best but better than the remaining two.
entries.source: Paul M. Fitts and C. M. Seeger, S-R compatibility: spatial characteristics of stimulus and response codes, Journal of Experimental Psychology 46(3), 199-210 (1953); Alphonse Chapanis and Lionel E. Lindenbaum, A Reaction Time Study of Four Control-Display Linkages, Human Factors 1(4), 1-7 (1959)

entries.title: Colour coding standards
entries.numbers: ISO 3864-1 (2011) design principles for safety signs and markings; ISO 3864-2 (2016) product safety labels, which adds orange for medium-level risk; ISO 3864-4 (2011) sets the colorimetric values. IEC 60204-1 clause 10.7.3 covers actuator colour. Around 8 per cent of men of northern European descent and about 0.5 per cent of women have red-green colour vision deficiency.
entries.source: ISO 3864 (parts 1 to 4); IEC 60204-1 clause 10.7.3; ISO 13850; NFPA 79

entries.title: Lifecycle and durability
entries.numbers: ISO 14040:2006 and ISO 14044:2006, four LCA phases. Phoebus cartel: founded 23 December 1924 in Geneva, 1,000-hour standard codified by early 1925, effective until 1940.
entries.source: ISO 14040:2006 and ISO 14044:2006; Markus Krajewski, The Great Lightbulb Conspiracy, IEEE Spectrum (24 September 2014)

entries.title: Levels of scale
entries.numbers: Alexander's summary of the property gives the step between neighbouring sizes as roughly 1:2 to 1:3, and warns against 1:5 or 1:10.
entries.source: Christopher Alexander, The Nature of Order, Book One: The Phenomenon of Life (2002)

entries.title: Pattern language
entries.numbers: 253 patterns in A Pattern Language (1977).
entries.source: Christopher Alexander, Sara Ishikawa and Murray Silverstein, A Pattern Language: Towns, Buildings, Construction (Oxford University Press, 1977)

entries.title: Enclosure ratios
entries.numbers: ITE and CNU (2010): enclosure is first perceived at about 1:4 height to width; 1:3 to 1:2 is described as appropriate enclosure in dense urban contexts.
entries.source: Institute of Transportation Engineers with the Congress for the New Urbanism, Designing Walkable Urban Thoroughfares: A Context Sensitive Approach (2010), figure 4.2

entries.title: Daylight and solar orientation
entries.numbers: BS EN 17037:2018 minimum target: 300 lux over 50 per cent of the reference plane and 100 lux over 95 per cent, for at least 50 per cent of daylight hours. BR 209 sunlight targets: at least 25 per cent annual probable sunlight hours and at least 5 per cent in winter, tested on windows within 90 degrees of due south.
entries.source: BS EN 17037:2018, Daylight in Buildings; BRE, Site Layout Planning for Daylight and Sunlight: A Guide to Good Practice (BR 209), Littlefair, 2022 edition

entries.title: Active frontage
entries.numbers: Gehl, Kaefer and Reigstad (2006): category A, 15-20 doors per 100 m; B, 10-14; C, 6-8; D, 2-5; E, 0-2. In the Copenhagen study, stops and other activity were seven times greater in front of active than passive facades, with a further 13 per cent of activity added by pedestrians slowing as they passed.
entries.source: Jan Gehl, Lotte Johansen Kaefer and Solvejg Reigstad, Close Encounters with Buildings, Urban Design International 11(1), 29-47 (2006); first published in Danish as Naerkontakt med huse, Arkitekten, September 2004

entries.title: Shearing layers (site, structure, skin, services, space plan, stuff)
entries.numbers: Brand's ranges: structure 30-300 years, skin about 20 years, services 7-15 years, space plan 3-30 years. Duffy's earlier four layers were shell 30-50 years, services 15 years, scenery 5 years, set weeks to months.
entries.source: Stewart Brand, How Buildings Learn: What Happens After They're Built (1994), extending Frank Duffy's four layers published in The Changing Workplace (1992)

entries.title: Problem framing and reframing
entries.numbers: Rittel and Webber list ten properties of a wicked problem.
entries.source: Rittel and Webber (1973); Buchanan (1992).

entries.title: Empathise, define, ideate, prototype, test
entries.numbers: Five modes.
entries.source: Hasso Plattner Institute of Design at Stanford, An Introduction to Design Thinking: Process Guide (2010).

entries.title: Human-centred design as a standard (ISO 9241-210)
entries.numbers: ISO 9241-210:2019 is the second edition, published July 2019.
entries.source: ISO 9241-210:2019, Ergonomics of human-system interaction, Part 210.

entries.title: User interviews
entries.numbers: Contextual inquiry sessions typically run about two hours one to one, with published sample sizes from four users for a single small task up to thirty or more.
entries.source: No single origin. Beyer and Holtzblatt's Contextual Design (1997) is the nearest formal grounding.

entries.title: Contextual inquiry
entries.numbers: About two hours per session; sample sizes from four users for one small task up to thirty or more.
entries.source: Hugh Beyer and Karen Holtzblatt, Contextual Design (1997).

entries.title: Diary studies
entries.numbers: NN/g suggests roughly 5 to 12 participants for a small discovery project, 12 to 30 for a large one and 30 to 50 for academic-scale work, with about one week for daily behaviours and about three weeks for weekly ones.
entries.source: Nielsen Norman Group, Diary Studies (checked 2026); experience sampling is the psychology term for the signal-based variant.

entries.title: Surveys
entries.numbers: SUS: ten items, five-point agreement scale, score 0 to 100, created 1986 and published 1996, mean 68 across 500 studies and over 5,000 users. NPS: 0 to 10 scale, with 9 and 10 counted as promoters and 0 to 6 as detractors.
entries.source: John Brooke, SUS: a quick and dirty usability scale (1996); Fred Reichheld, The One Number You Need to Grow (HBR, 2003); Keiningham and colleagues, Journal of Marketing (2007).

entries.title: Service blueprints
entries.numbers: One line in the original (visibility); four in the version usually taught, after Zeithaml and Bitner added three; a fifth, the line of order penetration, has been proposed since. Five common rows: customer actions, front-stage actions, back-stage actions, support processes, physical evidence.
entries.source: G. Lynn Shostack, Designing Services That Deliver, Harvard Business Review 62(1), January to February 1984, 133 to 139; later lines from Zeithaml and Bitner, Services Marketing (1996).

entries.title: Crazy eights and rapid ideation
entries.numbers: Eight sketches in eight minutes, done individually, per Google's Design Sprint Kit.
entries.source: Google Design Sprint Kit, Crazy 8's; the method is associated with Jake Knapp's design sprint work.

entries.title: SCAMPER
entries.numbers: Seven letters.
entries.source: Bob Eberle, SCAMPER: Games for Imagination Development (1971), built on Alex Osborn's Applied Imagination and on techniques from Frank E. Williams.

entries.title: Fidelity matched to the question
entries.numbers: Three dimensions: role, look and feel, implementation.
entries.source: Stephanie Houde and Charles Hill, What do Prototypes Prototype? (Apple Computer, 1997).

entries.title: Heuristic evaluation
entries.numbers: Three to five independent evaluators, per Nielsen Norman Group.
entries.source: Jakob Nielsen and Rolf Molich, CHI 1990; Nielsen and Landauer, INTERCHI 1993; Nielsen Norman Group guidance.

entries.title: Cognitive walkthrough
entries.numbers: Four questions per step in the original method; two in Spencer's 2000 version.
entries.source: Wharton, Rieman, Lewis and Polson, in Nielsen and Mack (eds), Usability Inspection Methods (1994); Spencer (2000).

entries.title: Moderated usability testing
entries.numbers: See entry 974 for sample size and what the numbers actually support.
entries.source: Nielsen Norman Group, Remote Usability Tests: Moderated and Unmoderated (checked 2026).

entries.title: The five-user rule and its limits
entries.numbers: Nielsen: L = 31 per cent, giving about 85 per cent of problems at five users; he separately advises 20 users for quantitative studies and 15 for card sorting. Faulkner 2003, from 60 users and 45 known problems: sets of five found between 55 and 99 per cent, mean 85.55; ten users found at least 82 per cent, mean 94.7; twenty users at least 95 per cent. Spool and Schroeder 2001: first five users found 35 per cent.
entries.source: Nielsen and Landauer, INTERCHI 1993; Jakob Nielsen, Why You Only Need to Test with 5 Users (2000); Laura Faulkner, Beyond the Five-User Assumption, Behavior Research Methods 35(3) (2003), 379 to 383; Spool and Schroeder, Testing Web Sites: Five Users Is Nowhere Near Enough, CHI 2001 Extended Abstracts, 285 to 286.

entries.title: Accessibility audit
entries.numbers: Five steps; a random sample set of 10 per cent of the structured sample size.
entries.source: W3C, WCAG Evaluation Methodology (WCAG-EM) 2.0, W3C Group Note (23 July 2026).

entries.title: A/B testing and its limits
entries.numbers: About one third of tested ideas at Microsoft improved their target metric (Kohavi, Crook and Longbotham, 2009).
entries.source: Ronny Kohavi, Thomas Crook and Roger Longbotham, Online Experimentation at Microsoft (2009); repeated in Kohavi, Tang and Xu, Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (2020).

entries.title: HEART framework
entries.numbers: Five metric categories; three steps in the goals, signals, metrics process.
entries.source: Kerry Rodden, Hilary Hutchinson and Xin Fu, CHI 2010 (Google).

entries.title: Decision records
entries.numbers: Five sections: title, context, decision, status, consequences.
entries.source: Michael Nygard, Documenting Architecture Decisions (15 November 2011).

entries.title: Iteration cadence
entries.numbers: Scrum Sprints are fixed length, one month or less, with no gap between them.
entries.source: Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, The Scrum Guide (2020).

entries.title: Dark pattern: bait and switch
entries.numbers: UK: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024, Schedule 20, paragraph 5 (bait advertising) and paragraph 6 (bait and switch). Schedule 20 lists 32 practices unfair in all circumstances and came into force on 6 April 2025.
entries.source: Harry Brignull, darkpatterns.org (2010) and Deceptive Patterns (2023); UK DMCC Act 2024, Schedule 20

entries.title: Dark pattern: roach motel
entries.numbers: EU Digital Services Act, Article 25(3)(c). GDPR, Article 7(3). In the US, the FTC's revised Negative Option Rule (the click-to-cancel rule) was vacated in its entirety by the Eighth Circuit in July 2025 on procedural grounds, days before it took full effect; the Restore Online Shoppers' Confidence Act still requires a simple cancellation mechanism.
entries.source: Harry Brignull, darkpatterns.org (2010), renamed Hard to Cancel at deceptive.design; EU DSA Article 25; GDPR Article 7

entries.title: Dark pattern: forced continuity
entries.numbers: Mathur et al. (2019) found 1,818 dark pattern instances across roughly 53,000 product pages on about 11,000 shopping sites, present on 1,254 sites (about 11.1 per cent), covering 15 types in 7 categories.
entries.source: Harry Brignull, darkpatterns.org (2010), renamed Hidden Subscription at deceptive.design; ROSCA (US, 2010)

entries.title: Dark pattern: disguised ads
entries.numbers: UK: DMCC Act 2024, Schedule 20, paragraph 12, covering paid editorial content that is not clearly identified.
entries.source: Harry Brignull, deceptive.design; UK DMCC Act 2024, Schedule 20 paragraph 12; FTC, Bringing Dark Patterns to Light (2022)

entries.title: Dark pattern: hidden costs
entries.numbers: UK: DMCC Act 2024 total price rule, in force 6 April 2025. The CMA has direct enforcement powers with fines up to 300,000 pounds or 10 per cent of worldwide turnover, whichever is higher.
entries.source: Harry Brignull, deceptive.design; UK DMCC Act 2024; CMA guidance CMA207, Unfair commercial practices

entries.title: Dark pattern: misdirection
entries.numbers: EU Digital Services Act, Article 25(3)(a). Mathur et al. (2019) list Misdirection as one of seven categories, containing four of their fifteen types.
entries.source: Harry Brignull, darkpatterns.org (2010), now split into Visual Interference and Trick Wording; Mathur et al. (2019); EU DSA Article 25

entries.title: Dark pattern: nagging
entries.numbers: EU Digital Services Act, Article 25(3)(b).
entries.source: Gray, Kou, Battles, Hoggatt and Toombs, The Dark (Patterns) Side of UX Design, CHI 2018; EU DSA Article 25

entries.title: Dark pattern: obstruction
entries.numbers: CMA definition of sludge: excessive or unjustified friction that makes it difficult for consumers to get what they want or to do as they wish.
entries.source: Gray et al., CHI 2018; Cass Sunstein on sludge; CMA, Evidence review of Online Choice Architecture (2022)

entries.title: Dark pattern: false urgency and scarcity
entries.numbers: UK: DMCC Act 2024, Schedule 20, paragraph 7. Mathur et al. (2019) found 157 deceptive countdown timers on 140 sites and 22 third-party entities offering dark patterns as a turnkey solution, across roughly 11,000 shopping sites.
entries.source: Harry Brignull, deceptive.design; Mathur et al. (2019); UK DMCC Act 2024, Schedule 20 paragraph 7

entries.title: Dark pattern: privacy zuckering
entries.numbers: GDPR, Article 25(2).
entries.source: Harry Brignull, darkpatterns.org (2010), term now retired; Gray et al., CHI 2018; GDPR Article 25(2)

entries.title: Honest consent design
entries.numbers: GDPR, Article 7 (conditions for consent), including Article 7(3) on withdrawal. EU Digital Services Act, Article 25.
entries.source: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR), Article 7; Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 (Digital Services Act), Article 25

entries.title: Data minimisation
entries.numbers: GDPR, Article 5(1)(c) and Article 25(2).
entries.source: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR), Articles 5 and 25

entries.title: Privacy by design
entries.numbers: Seven foundational principles (Cavoukian, 2009). GDPR, Article 25.
entries.source: Ann Cavoukian, Privacy by Design: The 7 Foundational Principles (2009); GDPR Article 25

entries.title: Honest defaults
entries.numbers: Johnson and Goldstein, Science 302, 1338-1339 (2003): nearly 60 percentage points between the opt-in and presumed-consent groups; 42 per cent consenting under an opt-in default against 82 per cent under opt-out in their 161-person online experiment; an estimated 16.3 per cent rise in actual donation, 14.1 to 16.4 per million. GDPR, Article 25(2).
entries.source: Eric J. Johnson and Daniel G. Goldstein, Do Defaults Save Lives?, Science (2003); Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein, Nudge (2008); GDPR Article 25(2)

entries.title: Cost of addiction mechanics
entries.numbers: Orben and Przybylski, Nature Human Behaviour 3, 173-182 (2019): n = 355,358; screen use explains at most 0.4 per cent of the variation in adolescent wellbeing.
entries.source: Amy Orben and Andrew K. Przybylski, Nature Human Behaviour (2019); Addictive Design, deceptive.design

entries.title: Inclusive representation in imagery
entries.numbers: Project #ShowUs: over 14,000 images, 200 photographers, 41 countries, per Getty Images (accessed 2026).
entries.source: Project #ShowUs (Getty Images, Dove and Girlgaze, 2019); no single canonical text

entries.title: Algorithmic transparency
entries.numbers: Six explanation types (ICO and Alan Turing Institute, 2020). GDPR, Articles 13 to 15, Article 22 and Recital 71.
entries.source: ICO and The Alan Turing Institute, Explaining decisions made with AI (Project ExplAIn, 2020); GDPR Article 22

entries.title: Error transparency
entries.numbers: Nielsen's ten heuristics: developed with Rolf Molich in 1990, refined in 1994 from an analysis of 249 usability problems.
entries.source: Jakob Nielsen, 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design, heuristic 9 (with Rolf Molich, 1990; current form 1994)

entries.title: Digital sustainability (page weight and energy)
entries.numbers: Median page view under SWDM v4 in 2024: about 0.37 gCO2e desktop, 0.33 gCO2e mobile. Mobile emission share at the 75th percentile: images 61.7 per cent, JavaScript 27.4 per cent, fonts 5.6 per cent, CSS 3.6 per cent, HTML 1.8 per cent. Median mobile page weight rose 594 per cent, or 1.7 MB, between June 2012 and June 2022; desktop rose 221 per cent.
entries.source: Sustainable Web Design Model v4 (sustainablewebdesign.org); HTTP Archive Web Almanac 2024, Sustainability chapter; W3C Web Sustainability Guidelines

entries.title: Designing for vulnerable users
entries.numbers: FCA FG21/1 (February 2021): four drivers of vulnerability, being health, life events, resilience and capability. The FCA's Financial Lives coronavirus panel survey of October 2020, quoted on its own guidance page, found 53 per cent of UK adults displaying a characteristic of vulnerability, up by more than 3 million people since February 2020.
entries.source: FCA, FG21/1 Guidance for firms on the fair treatment of vulnerable customers (February 2021)

entries.title: Safety by design and abuse resistance
entries.numbers: eSafety Commissioner Safety by Design: three principles.
entries.source: eSafety Commissioner (Australia), Safety by Design principles (promoted since 2018)

entries.title: First Things First position
entries.numbers: 1964: twenty-two signatories in total. 2000: 33 signatories, published in seven magazines.
entries.source: Ken Garland, First Things First (1964); First Things First 2000, published in Eye, Adbusters, Emigre and others (1999-2000)

entries.title: Design for the real world (social responsibility)
entries.numbers: First published 1971; translated into over twenty languages per the publisher's own description, and into twenty-three according to several booksellers quoting a later edition.
entries.source: Victor Papanek, Design for the Real World: Human Ecology and Social Change (1971)

entries.title: Exit parity
entries.numbers: GDPR Article 7(3). EU Digital Services Act Article 25(3)(c). ROSCA simple cancellation requirement.
entries.source: GDPR Article 7(3); EU Digital Services Act Article 25(3)(c); ROSCA (US, 2010)

entries.title: Synthetic media disclosure
entries.numbers: EU AI Act, Article 50, applying from 2 August 2026, with the Article 50(2) machine-readable marking duty deferred to 2 December 2026 for generative systems already on the market before that date. Penalties up to 15 million euros or 3 per cent of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher.
entries.source: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 50; European Commission guidelines on Article 50 transparency obligations and Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated Content (July 2026)

entries.title: 45-75 characters per line (66 ideal)
entries.numbers: 45 to 75 characters is the accepted band and 66 the traditional target (Bringhurst 2.1.2). WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.8, level AAA, requires a mechanism for text blocks no wider than 80 characters, or 40 for CJK.
entries.source: Robert Bringhurst, The Elements of Typographic Style, section 2.1.2; W3C WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.8

entries.title: Body line-height 1.4-1.6
entries.numbers: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.12 (AA): no loss of content or functionality with line height at least 1.5 times font size, letter spacing 0.12 times, word spacing 0.16 times, and space after paragraphs 2 times. SC 1.4.8 (AAA): line spacing at least space-and-a-half within paragraphs. CSS line-height normal resolves to roughly 1.2 on desktop browsers (MDN).
entries.source: W3C WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.12 and SC 1.4.8; MDN Web Docs, CSS line-height; the 1.4-1.6 band itself has no traceable origin

entries.title: 16px minimum body text on the web
entries.numbers: Browsers resolve the CSS keyword medium to 16px by default. iOS Safari zooms on focus when an input's font-size is under 16px. WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.4 requires resize to 200 per cent and sets no minimum size.
entries.source: No standard sets it. MDN Web Docs, CSS font-size; W3C WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.4; documented iOS Safari input-zoom behaviour

entries.title: 4.5:1 contrast for body text
entries.numbers: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.3 (AA): 4.5:1 for text, 3:1 for large-scale text. SC 1.4.6 (AAA): 7:1 and 4.5:1. Large scale is at least 18 point, or 14 point bold.
entries.source: W3C WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.3 and SC 1.4.6 (W3C Recommendation, 2023)

entries.title: 3:1 contrast for large text and UI components
entries.numbers: 3:1 for large-scale text (SC 1.4.3, AA) and 3:1 for user interface components and graphical objects (SC 1.4.11, AA). Large scale is at least 18 point, or 14 point bold.
entries.source: W3C WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.3 and SC 1.4.11 (SC 1.4.11 introduced in WCAG 2.1, 2018)

entries.title: 24x24 minimum target, 44x44 comfortable
entries.numbers: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 (AA): 24 by 24 CSS pixels, with a spacing exception based on a 24-pixel-diameter circle. SC 2.5.5 (AAA): 44 by 44 CSS pixels. Apple HIG: default control size 44 by 44 points on iOS and iPadOS, minimum 28 by 28 points. Material Design: at least 48 by 48 dp with at least 8dp between targets.
