entries.source: W3C WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 and SC 2.5.5; Apple Human Interface Guidelines, Accessibility; Google Material Design, Spacing methods

entries.title: 8-point spacing grid
entries.numbers: Material Design: 8dp square baseline grid for all components across mobile, tablet and desktop; 4dp grid for icons, type and some in-component elements; type on a 4dp baseline grid. Material's own padding examples are measured in increments of 8dp or 4dp.
entries.source: Google Material Design, Spacing methods; The 8-Point Grid, spec.fm/specifics/8-pt-grid (undated, attributed to Bryn Jackson)

entries.title: 60-30-10 colour split
entries.numbers: 60 per cent dominant, 30 per cent secondary, 10 per cent accent. No published source, so treat the figures as an approximate budget rather than a specification.
entries.source: Origin unclear. Widely repeated in interior design and interface writing with no traceable originator.

entries.title: 0.1s, 1s, 10s response thresholds
entries.numbers: 0.1 second for direct manipulation, 1 second for uninterrupted flow, 10 seconds for the limit of attention on a task (Nielsen 1993, after Miller 1968 and Card et al. 1991).
entries.source: Jakob Nielsen, Response Times: The 3 Important Limits, Nielsen Norman Group (1 January 1993), an excerpt from chapter 5 of his Usability Engineering

entries.title: 100-500ms interface motion
entries.numbers: Most animations 100 to 500ms; simple feedback such as a checkbox around 100ms; substantial screen changes such as a modal 200 to 300ms; 100 to 400ms in most cases, with 400ms only for big movements across large screens (Laubheimer, NN/g, 2020).
entries.source: Page Laubheimer, Executing UX Animations: Duration and Motion Characteristics, Nielsen Norman Group (9 February 2020)

entries.title: 7+/-2 and the stricter 4+/-1
entries.numbers: Miller 1956: immediate memory span about seven items; span of absolute judgement a mean of 2.6 bits, which is about 6.5 categories, ranging over 3 to 15 across the studies he pooled. Cowan 2001: about four chunks. No published figure caps the number of items in a menu.
entries.source: George A. Miller, Psychological Review 63(2), 1956; Nelson Cowan, Behavioral and Brain Sciences 24(1), 2001; Jean-luc Doumont, IEEE Transactions on Professional Communication 45(2), 2002

entries.title: LCP 2.5s, INP 200ms, CLS 0.1
entries.numbers: Good thresholds: LCP 2.5 seconds or less, INP 200ms or less, CLS 0.1 or less, each measured at the 75th percentile of page loads and split between mobile and desktop.
entries.source: Google, Core Web Vitals, web.dev (INP replaced FID as a stable Core Web Vital in 2024)

entries.title: Type scale ratios 1.125 to 1.618
entries.source: Tim Brown, More Meaningful Typography, A List Apart (3 May 2011), building on Robert Bringhurst on scales

entries.title: Golden ratio 1.618, root-2 1.414
entries.numbers: Golden ratio 1.6180339887..., equal to (1 + root 5) / 2. Root two 1.41421356... ISO 216: A0 is 841 by 1189mm with an area of one square metre; A4 is 210 by 297mm.
entries.source: ISO 216 (after Lichtenberg 1786, Porstmann, DIN 476 1921); George Markowsky, Misconceptions about the Golden Ratio, The College Mathematics Journal 23(1), 1992, 2-19; Mario Livio, The Golden Ratio (2002)

entries.title: Adult reading speed, about 240 words a minute
entries.numbers: 238 wpm silent non-fiction and 260 wpm fiction, from 190 studies and 18,573 participants; typical ranges 175 to 300 wpm for non-fiction and 200 to 320 for fiction; 183 wpm read aloud, from a separate 77 studies and 5,965 participants (Brysbaert 2019).
entries.source: Marc Brysbaert, How many words do we read per minute? A review and meta-analysis of reading rate, Journal of Memory and Language 109 (2019), article 104047

entries.title: No spacing scale (arbitrary numbers)
entries.numbers: Material Design 2: 8dp square baseline grid for all components; 4dp grid available to icons, type and elements within components; padding in increments of 8dp or 4dp.
entries.source: Google, Material Design 2, Spacing methods (m2.material.io)

entries.title: Low-contrast grey on grey
entries.numbers: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.3 (AA): 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text (18pt, or 14pt bold). SC 1.4.11 (AA): 3:1 for user interface components and graphical objects. WebAIM Million 2026: low-contrast text on 83.9 per cent of one million home pages, with 56.1 detected errors per page on average.
entries.source: W3C, WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.3 and SC 1.4.11 (2023); WebAIM Million 2026

entries.title: Text on busy imagery without a scrim
entries.numbers: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.3 still applies over images: 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text.
entries.source: W3C, WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.3; Google, Material Design (scrim)

entries.title: Icon-only buttons with ambiguous meaning
entries.numbers: WebAIM Million 2026: empty buttons on 30.6 per cent of one million home pages. WCAG 2.2 SC 4.1.2 (Level A) and SC 2.5.3 Label in Name (Level A).
entries.source: Aurora Harley, Icon Usability, Nielsen Norman Group (27 July 2014); W3C, WCAG 2.2 SC 4.1.2 and SC 2.5.3

entries.title: Carousels as a content dumping ground
entries.numbers: nd.edu, Oct 2012 to Jan 2013: about 1 per cent of visitors clicked a feature; 84 per cent of the 28,928 clicks were on position 1. NN/g: five frames or fewer. WCAG 2.2 SC 2.2.2 (Level A): a pause, stop or hide mechanism for automatic movement lasting more than five seconds.
entries.source: Erik Runyon, Carousel Interaction Stats (January 2013); Kara Pernice, Designing Effective Carousels, Nielsen Norman Group (14 September 2013)

entries.title: Hover-dependent interactions
entries.numbers: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.13 (Level AA): additional content triggered by hover or focus must be dismissable, hoverable and persistent.
entries.source: W3C, WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.13 (2023); Aurora Harley, Icon Usability, Nielsen Norman Group (2014)

entries.title: Disabled buttons with no explanation
entries.numbers: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.3 exception: text that is part of an inactive user interface component has no contrast requirement.
entries.source: GOV.UK Design System, Button component; W3C, WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.3 (2023)

entries.title: Generic stock imagery
entries.numbers: Nielsen (2010), one user's eyetracking session on the FreshBooks team page: 10 per cent more time on the portrait photos than on the biographies, which occupied 316 per cent more space. Not a multi-user average.
entries.source: Jakob Nielsen, Photos as Web Content, Nielsen Norman Group (31 October 2010)

entries.title: Mixed corner radii
entries.numbers: Nested radius formula: inner radius = outer radius - padding (equivalently, outer = inner + padding).
entries.source: Craft convention; the nesting formula is documented by Paul Hebert, The Math Behind Nesting Rounded Corners, Cloud Four (26 October 2022).

entries.title: Decorative motion with no purpose
entries.numbers: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.2.2 (Level A): five seconds. SC 2.3.3 (Level AAA). CSS prefers-reduced-motion values: no-preference, reduce.
entries.source: W3C, WCAG 2.2 SC 2.2.2 and SC 2.3.3 (2023); CSS Media Queries Level 5, prefers-reduced-motion

entries.title: Audio that plays automatically
entries.numbers: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.2 Audio Control (Level A): automatic audio lasting more than 3 seconds requires a pause or stop mechanism, or an independent volume control.
entries.source: W3C, WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.2 Audio Control (2023)

entries.title: Asking for data you don't need
entries.numbers: Baymard Institute: average checkout form fields 12.7 (2019), 11.8 (2021), 11.3 (2024); most sites need only 8. GDPR Article 5(1)(c): data minimisation.
entries.source: Baymard Institute checkout research; Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR), Article 5(1)(c)

entries.title: Error messages that blame the user
entries.numbers: WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.1 Error Identification (Level A); SC 3.3.3 Error Suggestion (Level AA).
entries.source: Jakob Nielsen, 10 Usability Heuristics (1994), heuristic 9; Tim Neusesser and Evan Sunwall, Error-Message Guidelines, Nielsen Norman Group (14 May 2023); W3C, WCAG 2.2

entries.title: Placeholder text used as a label
entries.numbers: WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.2 (Level A). WebAIM Million 2026: missing form input labels on 51 per cent of one million home pages.
entries.source: W3C WAI, Forms tutorial, User instructions; Katie Sherwin, Placeholders in Form Fields Are Harmful, Nielsen Norman Group (11 May 2014); WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.2

entries.title: Walls of undifferentiated text
entries.numbers: Nielsen (1997): 79 per cent of users always scanned; 16 per cent read word by word. Measured usability improvements: concise 58 per cent, scannable 47 per cent, objective language 27 per cent, combined 124 per cent.
entries.source: Jakob Nielsen, How Users Read on the Web, Nielsen Norman Group (30 September 1997), reporting work with John Morkes

entries.title: Text touching a rule or an edge
entries.numbers: No single standard. Bleed and quiet-zone allowances are set by the printer and by the product. Marqetspace: 1.5mm bleed and a 4mm quiet zone on most products; 3mm bleed and at least a 10mm quiet zone on booklets. Inprint Group: 3mm bleed.
entries.source: Print trade practice; individual printers publish their own bleed and quiet-zone specifications, for example the Marqetspace file supply guide.

entries.title: Inaccessible custom controls
entries.numbers: WCAG 2.2 SC 4.1.2 (Level A); SC 2.5.3 Label in Name (Level A). WebAIM Million 2026: ARIA on 82.7 per cent of home pages; 59.1 average errors with ARIA versus 42 without.
entries.source: W3C, WCAG 2.2 SC 4.1.2 and SC 2.5.3 (2023); W3C WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices Guide; WebAIM Million 2026

entries.title: Removing the focus indicator
entries.numbers: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.7 Focus Visible (Level AA). SC 2.4.13 Focus Appearance (Level AAA): at least a 2 CSS pixel thick perimeter equivalent, and at least 3:1 contrast between focused and unfocused states.

entries.title: Non-responsive tables
entries.numbers: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.10 (Level AA): 320 CSS pixels wide for vertical scrolling content, 256 CSS pixels high for horizontal. The W3C notes 320 CSS pixels corresponds to a 1280px window at 400 per cent zoom. Data tables are named in the exception.
entries.source: W3C, WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.10 Reflow and its Understanding document (2023)

entries.title: Layout shift on load
entries.numbers: CLS: 0.1 or less is good, above 0.25 is poor, assessed at the 75th percentile of page loads. Session window: shifts less than one second apart, five second maximum window. Score = impact fraction x distance fraction.
entries.source: Google, Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS), web.dev

entries.title: Fake progress indicators
entries.numbers: Harrison et al., UIST 2007, pages 115 to 118: bars held at a constant 5.5 seconds. Buell and Norton, Management Science 57(9), 2011, pages 1564 to 1579: five experiments.
entries.source: Chris Harrison, Brian Amento, Stacey Kuznetsov and Robert Bell, Rethinking the Progress Bar, UIST 2007; Ryan W. Buell and Michael I. Norton, The Labor Illusion, Management Science 57(9), 2011; Qihan Wang, Xinyue Kang and Pei-Luen Patrick Rau, The Magic of Slow-to-Fast and Constant, arXiv:2211.13909 (2022)

entries.title: Truncation with no route to the full text
entries.numbers: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.10 (Level AA): content presented without loss of information at a width equivalent to 320 CSS pixels.
entries.source: W3C, WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.10 (2023); MDN Web Docs, text-overflow

entries.title: The model default (the AI look)
entries.numbers: None. West's article gives no measurement, and no study of the convergence was found. The claim rests on observation.
entries.source: Alan West, Why Every AI-Built Website Looks the Same (Blame Tailwind's Indigo-500), dev.to, 25 March 2026; Jack Pearce, Where does that purple gradient come from?, jackpearce.co.uk (undated note); the composite is the failure modes at #1027, #1048, #1030, #1025, #1039, #1040 and #1041

entries.title: Perceived performance
entries.numbers: Nielsen's response bands, from Miller (1968) and Card et al. (1991): 0.1 second feels instantaneous, 1 second maintains flow of thought, 10 seconds is the limit of held attention.
entries.source: R. B. Miller, Response Time in Man-Computer Conversational Transactions (1968); Jakob Nielsen, Usability Engineering (1993), chapter 5.

entries.title: Determinate versus indeterminate progress
entries.numbers: Myers (CHI 1985): 48 subjects, mostly computer science graduate students with about one fifth computer novices; 86.1 per cent liked progress indicators, mean usefulness rating 2.94 on a scale where 1 is very useful and 9 is useless and annoying. Delays were held at a constant 10 seconds or varied randomly from 1 to 17 seconds, so the indicator changed no actual duration. Nielsen: past about 10 seconds, show a percent-done indicator and give a clearly signposted way to interrupt the operation.
entries.source: Brad A. Myers, The importance of percent-done progress indicators for computer-human interfaces, CHI (1985); Jakob Nielsen, Usability Engineering (1993).

entries.title: Inline validation timing
entries.numbers: Wroblewski and Etre (2009), 22 participants: inline validation gave a 22 per cent increase in success rates, a 22 per cent decrease in errors, a 31 per cent increase in satisfaction ratings, a 42 per cent decrease in completion times and a 47 per cent decrease in eye fixations, compared with submit-and-refresh validation.
entries.source: Luke Wroblewski with Etre, Inline Validation in Web Forms, A List Apart (2009); Mihael Konjevic, Inline validation in forms: designing the experience, for the reward early, punish late pattern.

entries.title: Tooltip use and misuse
entries.numbers: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.13 Content on Hover or Focus is level AA and has three conditions: dismissible, hoverable, persistent.
entries.source: W3C, WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.4.13 Content on Hover or Focus (level AA).

entries.title: Scroll affordance and depth cues
entries.numbers: NN/g eyetracking (2018), 120 participants and over 130,000 fixations: 57 per cent of viewing time above the fold, 74 per cent within the first two screenfuls. The equivalent 2010 figure for above the fold was 80 per cent.
entries.source: Tom Brinck, Darren Gergle and Scott D. Wood, Designing Web Sites that Work: Usability for the Web (Morgan Kaufmann, 2002), for the false bottom; Nielsen Norman Group, Scrolling and Attention (2018), for the attention figures.

entries.title: Sticky elements
entries.numbers: Nielsen Norman Group cite a 13:1 content-to-chrome ratio on an iPhone 11 Pro as reasonable and 2:1 as poor, and suggest a 300 to 400ms slide-in for headers that reappear. Apple's Human Interface Guidelines set a minimum hit region of 44x44 pt (60x60 pt in visionOS), which puts a practical floor under bar height.
entries.source: Page Laubheimer, Sticky Headers: 5 Ways to Make Them Better, Nielsen Norman Group (4 April 2021). The 22 per cent figure is from Hyrum Denney, A Sticky Menu Is Quicker To Navigate, Smashing Magazine (11 September 2012).

entries.title: Drag-and-drop feedback
entries.numbers: WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.5.7 Dragging Movements, Level AA. WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), Level AA, sets 24 by 24 CSS pixels; Apple's Human Interface Guidelines ask for 44 by 44 pt.
entries.source: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.2, Success Criterion 2.5.7 Dragging Movements (Level AA).

entries.title: Label placement in forms
entries.numbers: Penzo measured saccade times, the eye movement from label to field: about 500ms for left-aligned labels beside the field, 170ms for experts and 240ms for novices with right-aligned labels beside the field, and 50ms with labels above the field. Setting those top labels in bold pushed 50ms up to 80ms. These are the real figures behind the claim, and they come from one small study.
entries.source: Matteo Penzo, Label Placement in Forms, UXmatters (12 July 2006), popularised by Luke Wroblewski in Web Form Design: Filling in the Blanks, Rosenfeld Media (2008).

entries.title: Input masks and formatting
entries.numbers: Baymard Institute report that 89 per cent of users are likely to enter numerical inputs in several different ways even when a formatting example is shown, that 98 per cent of e-commerce sites restrict inputs on certain fields, and that 64 per cent of sites either do not use input masks or use them incorrectly.
entries.source: Edward Scott, Consider Using Localized Input Masks for 'Phone' and Other Restricted Inputs, Baymard Institute (28 November 2017).

entries.title: Smart defaults and autofill
entries.numbers: WCAG 2.1 and 2.2 Success Criterion 1.3.5 Identify Input Purpose, Level AA. The valid values are the fixed autocomplete tokens in the HTML standard, not free text.
entries.source: W3C, WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.3.5 Identify Input Purpose, and the HTML standard's autofill field names. Defaults as a design principle are covered separately at 583.

entries.title: Multi-step forms and progress indication
entries.numbers: In Kivetz, Urminsky and Zheng's cafe field experiment, customers given a 12-stamp card carrying two free bonus stamps completed the same ten purchases in 12.7 days on average, against 15.6 days for customers given a plain 10-stamp card.
entries.source: GOV.UK Design System question pages pattern (progress indicators). Goal-gradient evidence from Ran Kivetz, Oleg Urminsky and Yuhuang Zheng, The Goal-Gradient Hypothesis Resurrected, Journal of Marketing Research 43(1), pp. 39-58 (2006).

entries.title: Error summary and field-level errors
entries.numbers: WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 3.3.1 Error Identification (Level A) and 3.3.3 Error Suggestion (Level AA).
entries.source: GOV.UK Design System error summary and error message components; W3C WCAG 2.2 Success Criteria 3.3.1 and 3.3.3.

entries.title: Primary, secondary and tertiary action hierarchy
entries.numbers: Apple's Human Interface Guidelines advise keeping prominent buttons to one or two per view.
entries.source: Apple, Human Interface Guidelines, Buttons (Style and Role sections).

entries.title: Disabled-state pitfalls
entries.numbers: WCAG 2.2 Success Criteria 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) and 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast both exempt inactive user interface components from contrast requirements.
entries.source: W3C, WCAG 2.2 Understanding documents for Success Criteria 1.4.3 and 1.4.11 (Inactive User Interface Components).

entries.title: Notification restraint
entries.numbers: Apple's Human Interface Guidelines define four notification interruption levels: passive, active (the default), time sensitive and critical. Only time sensitive and critical break through a Focus; only critical overrides the Ring and Silent switch. Time sensitive is meant for something happening now or within an hour.
entries.source: Apple, Human Interface Guidelines, Managing notifications. The entitlement requirement for critical alerts comes from Apple's separate developer entitlement process, not from this page.

entries.title: Personalisation versus predictability
entries.numbers: Twenty-seven participants. Asked which menu they preferred overall, 55 per cent chose adaptable, 30 per cent adaptive and 15 per cent static, even though the static split menu was the optimal one. Sixteen of the twenty-seven also judged adaptable the most efficient, and exactly one person found it the most frustrating.
entries.source: Leah Findlater and Joanna McGrenere, A Comparison of Static, Adaptive, and Adaptable Menus, CHI (2004).

entries.title: Timeouts and session expiry
entries.numbers: WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable, Level A. The criterion's extension route requires warning the user, giving at least 20 seconds to respond with a simple action, and allowing extension at least ten times. Limits over 20 hours are exempt.
entries.source: W3C, WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable (Level A).
